lines.en: Several hours later, a girl who missed the earlier ordeal was treating herself to a much deserved moment of respite following a marathon of other moments that could only be described as “wack.”
It’d been a tough week for her, following a tough month of a tough year in an overwhelmingly tough life. But she would not let this dissuade her from her primary purpose in all of this.
To live and be happy. To love and be free. And to find a place to rest her bones that would not send her steamrolling down a train of thought scheduled to stop at “I never should have come here.”
That’s where she’d get off, though. And she’d find a place to sit and attempt to convince herself she wasn’t lied to when her hopes had been lifted just a short while ago.
Twenty-four hours had passed since she’d arrived here and she hadn’t even heard a word from the only voice she’d come to love.

Unbeknownst to her, however, this place brought a lingering sting for the man of her dreams that was only exacerbated by the fact that she was sitting on the same rock where he once told her he loved her.
That her wasn’t her to him, though. But lately, he hadn’t been him to her either. So he and she had a lot of experimenting to do if she and he were ever going to work things out.
This was not the place for that, though.
In fact, some would say this is the worst place for that.
And while the roof of the school had gained notoriety in recent years as the widely proclaimed “edge of the world,” that had never been and never will be true.
The real edge is here — just across the water. And if you listen carefully, you might even hear a school bell or two creeping up from the bottom of the world beneath yours.
But of course she couldn’t. Wouldn’t. For she’d misplaced her mind and her heart in a dark concrete room that she would never escape. Even when she did.
And maybe one day, she’d summon the resolve to swim out as far as the eye can see, then even further than that. Until she falls off the edge and starts all over in a brand new ocean.
Oh, how she wished her lifeguard would come. And oh, how he refused to — for she was now the same as everyone else.

And the only one who was special was the girl she’d grown to envy with every ounce of her decrepit heart — who laced her venom with sedatives so the congealing of her blood would dance alongside drowsiness and sing her to sleep.
They were friends, once upon a time.
But now?
The girl had no idea.
: What are you looking at?
Also unbeknownst to her, there was a second girl who’d been here all along — thinking nicer thoughts than yesterday now that she’d escaped his/His range.
: Uhh...hi?
The mind of the second girl wasn’t all good, though. And while it remained purer than most, there was still the matter of addressing an unmistakable darkness bubbling up within it.
She was compelled to expel this darkness. But she’d learned in recent times that listening to the voices in her head was not always good.
This made her feel young again in the worst way possible. And she’d live in perpetual misery from this point on, knowing that just being herself would always hurt someone else.
In this moment, however, she thought less of the pain she may inflict on others and focused solely on a new premonition. Or a “secret” as the rabbits called it.
To Yasu, it was nothing but the truth.
To Maya, it was an unbelievable lie.
: Why are you all alone?...Shouldn’t you be with your friends?
: Shouldn’t you not be spying on people? What happened to the leash Touka keeps you on? You’re not lost, are you?
: Yes and no. But it’s everyone else who is even more lost, for the Light will always guide me home and neglect to even show itself to others.
: Or...most others at least.
: This isn’t another recruitment speech, is it? Because I’ve already pledged to show up weekly to a shrine I don’t believe in and I’m not sure I have enough time for a church as well.
: This is no recruitment, but a warning.
: A warning? What kind of warning?
: Bad things will happen if you stay here. You need to leave as soon as possible.
: But I’m afraid I can’t tell you any more than that as this secret must be kept from God as well.
: Ahh, okay. So you’re the heretic this time and I’m just the girl you chose to wash your feet.
: I’m afraid I don’t understand what you mean. Faithless lies from other schools of belief do nothing but bounce off of the cage He locked my mind inside of.
: This whole damn world is a cage, Yasu. You think you’ll find happiness just staying locked inside of it for the rest of forever?
: Not at all — for I will get to leave one day. And Asbeel tells me you will not.
: Okay...and who the hell is Asbeel?
: A friend...who hears whispers of the end of days and cares enough to share them with us despite the penalties and pain it feels for doing so.
: And this friend of yours just so happened to tell you that I am a momentous figure in your latest prediction? Despite never having actually met me?
: That is correct.
: And you expect me to believe you?
: No...I do not.
: Then why tell me at all? I’m pretty clearly trying to get some privacy over here. If I wanted to hear a sermon, I’d have come to you.
: Because I am a messenger...and it is my duty to spread the truth regardless of how harsh that truth may be. But also...
: Because I don’t want to hear it happen...
: And I fear what it will do to the one meant to deliver us to salvation.
: Don’t want to hear what happen, though? Just “bad things” doesn’t really give me anything to go off of. And listening to some psycho just makes me look like an idiot in the end.
: It’s better to be an idiot than to be nothing at all...isn’t it?
: Sure. Whatever. Message delivered. Now, can you leave me alone and go back to your handler?
: I already have to deal with a time-traveling rapist and her equally rapey uncle every day. Adding a cultist to the mix just makes it feel like I’m part of the world’s worst sitcom.
: A sitcom...
: Yes...you are not far off at all.
: Tell me, Maya — do you know how to swim?
: Or are you more the “drowning” type?...
: The sky looks rather...ominous out there, doesn’t it?
: I wonder if it’s going to rain?
: Do you like the rain, Touka?
: I’m not sure I feel one way or the other about it. I suppose it’s convenient that I have my swimsuit on should it start to come down, though.
: I like the rain. Though, I’m not quite sure I can explain why.
: That’s quite odd coming from someone like you. I believed there to be nothing you’d struggle to put into words.
: That just means you don’t know the first thing about me.
: Sometimes, I think I struggle with that more than anything at all.
: To be completely honest, I’m not sure how I would know anything about you when the two of us have barely ever talked at all.
: I’m willing to learn, though. Should you oblige me, that is.
: I’m a daughter. Apart from that, I’m not sure what else I’d tell you that you haven’t already discerned in school.
: Mm. I figured as much was implied. But I’m glad to have found some common ground with you, however small it may be. For I, too, am a daughter.
: And to a quite interesting mother at that.
: Tell me — do you ever brush her hair?
: My mother’s? No...She has attendants to do that should the need arise. Which it doesn’t very often seeing as it’s short and easily manageable. Likely to save her time, I presume.
: I see. But would you if she asked?
: Of course. I love my mother dearly despite her...peculiar outlook on fringe topics directly relevant to my life.
: Then I assume you’d do it without asking as well if she lost her ability to speak?
: May I ask the purpose for this rather odd line of questioning, Nodoka? Is this something you do with all of the girls that I was simply not aware of?
: Not really. I’m just feeling somewhat melancholic. Like I’ve exhausted myself by failing too many times. And I’m beginning to ponder why it is I still persist so adamantly despite that.
: I suppose that’s just the type of girl you are. One who doesn’t simply back down when things become too tough.
: It’s not even that it’s tough. There are few questions out there I’m incapable of answering. It’s figuring out what to ask that’s difficult sometimes. That is what I struggle with.
: Well, I’m sure it won’t help your melancholy, but I’m somewhat delighted to know that you struggle at all and are not as perfect as you present yourself.
: You think I’m perfect? Why?
: You’re a beautiful genius with no visible weakness. If that’s not the textbook definition of perfect, I don’t know what is.
: Having all the required or desirable elements, qualities, or characteristics; as good as it is possible to be.
: Right. That. Precisely that.
: Did I say something funny? Your expression changed.
: It’s less what was said and more how you said it. Though, I suppose I shouldn’t blame you for being unable to find the humor in it when I often struggle with the same myself.
: I see. Then the two of us have uncovered additional common ground and you can continue to expand upon the reasons you like me.
: I do hope it’s not a one-way street, though. The last thing I’d want is to be on the unrequited end of yet another friendship.
: You want to be friends?
: I would not be opposed.
: If we’re friends, can I visit your home unsupervised? Or do I need to ask you before I come over?
: Is there...a reason you want to visit my house unsupervised?
: You’re not planning on robbing me, are you? Because I have many guards, Nodoka. You would be shockingly unsuccessful in such an endeavor despite your genius.
: It would be easiest if you were to just tell me everything you know about the everblooming sakura in your mother’s botanical garden.
: The sakura? Why do you want to know about that?
: Because it’s one of many things in this world that defies logic. Sakura rarely bloom for more than two weeks as they rely on a multitude of factors that can’t be replicated by mere gardening.
: Even if you were able to properly recreate the perfect weather cycle for one, which I’m sure is well within your family's capabilities, you’d need to change the life cycle of the petals themselves.
: There’s pollination as well and I’ve heard nothing of your family keeping bees. Are you handling that artificially? Is the tree genetically engineered? And also, is someone buried underneath it?
: Buried under- what?! Did my younger sister tell you that blasted rumor?
: Because Mother told her to stop spreading misinformation among the peasants and it appears as if she’s neglected to heed her warning once more.
: It’s not true then?
: Of course it isn’t true. That’s ridiculous. I can’t believe Tsukasa-
: Your sister didn’t tell me anything.
: What? Then...someone else from the-
: No one told me anything.
: Then...where did this come from? Why would you even think such a thing?
: A poem. Written by Ami’s mother.
: Ami’s...what? Excuse me?
: I don’t particularly like poems.
: I feel as if, more often than not, they’re too easy to understand. And I much prefer the work associated with deciphering a good novel or short story instead.
: But someone my mother knew loved them, so I’ve casually consumed the medium in my spare time over the years when there’s nothing else available.
: Right, yes. I understand that. But you’re saying Ami’s mother-
: Is an infamous poet from right here in Kumon-mi who mysteriously vanished about eight years ago. But of course, we know that she didn’t vanish at all. She died.
: And before she died, she wrote one final poem dedicated to the love of her life called “The Tree That Blooms Forever” in which I believe your family’s sakura is mentioned.
: It sucks. Most of her later work did, in my opinion. But this one was short enough to memorize, and it goes like this.
: I’ve lost, my love. It’s over. But when I’m gone, don’t weep.\n‘Neath the tree that blooms forever, I’m not gone. I’m just asleep.
: And you think...that’s our tree she’s referring to?
: I do.
: Nodoka...What on earth would Ami’s mother have to do with my family?
: I was hoping you’d be able to tell me that as well. This isn’t something I can uncover through research alone.
: I’m sorry, but...I believe you’re mistaken. There’s nothing of the sort buried beneath that tree.
: I suppose I know where the rumors come from now, though...
: I see.
: I was hoping to avoid asking Sensei, but it appears I may have to now.
: Um...don’t? You know as well as I do that the slightest hint of tragedy sends that man spiraling downward faster than a peregrine falcon.
: You know about birds, Touka?
: A...fair bit. Why do you ask? Is there a poem about those as well?
: Oh, yes. Many. But I don’t intend to ask you about or recite any of them.
: I just want to know which one you see yourself as.
: I’ve always thought of myself as a white-fronted parrot.
Nodoka’s affection has increased to [nodoka_love]!
